question: Which specific white blood cells does HIV target and attack inside the body?
explanation: Spot on! HIV locks onto CD4+ T lymphocytes. As it infects and damages these cells over time, the body's immune system gradually weakens. You've got this! [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h1)

question: Why do patients living with HIV take a combination of multiple antiretroviral drugs instead of just one?

options.A: To prevent the virus from quickly developing drug resistance
options.B: To completely cure the virus within a few weeks
options.C: To prevent the drugs from causing any side effects
options.D: To make the pills easier to swallow every morning

explanation: Great thinking! HIV changes shape very easily. Using a combination of drugs that attack the virus from different angles stops it from mutating and overpowering the treatment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h1)

question: What does the clinical term 'undetectable viral load' mean for a patient on ART?

options.A: The immune system has stopped producing white blood cells
options.B: The virus has completely disappeared from every organ in the body
options.C: The amount of HIV in the blood is too low for standard lab tests to measure
options.D: The patient no longer needs to take their daily medications

explanation: An undetectable viral load means the medication has successfully suppressed the virus so standard blood tests cannot find it. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h2)

question: A patient with an undetectable viral load for over a year asks if they can still pass the virus sexually. What is the best response?

options.A: Transmission can only happen if they stop eating fresh fruits
options.B: They can only transmit the virus during the rainy season
options.C: Transmission is still just as likely as before starting treatment
options.D: The risk of sexual transmission is effectively zero as long as adherence is maintained

explanation: Brilliant! This is what we call U=U (Undetectable equals Untransmittable). When a patient takes their meds and stays undetectable, they cannot pass the virus sexually. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h2)

question: How do Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs) stop HIV from multiplying?

options.A: By destroying red blood cells in the bloodstream
options.B: By preventing viral DNA from inserting into the host cell's DNA
options.C: By changing the patient's blood type permanently
options.D: By blocking the patient from feeling hungry

explanation: You got it! INSTIs block the 'integrase' enzyme, which the virus uses like glue to paste its own genetic code into our human cells. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h3)

question: Which drug class works by acting as faulty building blocks that trick the reverse transcriptase enzyme?
explanation: Well done! NRTIs send in fake building blocks. The virus gets tricked into using them, which completely halts the creation of its viral DNA. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h3)

question: Which medication is a core part of the preferred first-line ART treatment for adults in Nigeria?
explanation: Correct! Dolutegravir is a powerful, safe integrase inhibitor that forms the backbone of standard first-line HIV treatment in Nigeria today. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h4)

question: When is a patient usually switched from a first-line ART regimen to a second-line regimen?

options.A: Whenever the patient travels to a different state
options.B: After the patient has taken their medication for exactly one month
options.C: When treatment failure is confirmed by a persistently high viral load
options.D: As soon as the patient reports a mild headache

explanation: Spot on! If a patient takes their drugs well, but lab tests keep showing a high viral load, it means the first drugs are failing and it's time to switch regimens. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h4)

question: Why do nurses check kidney function (like serum creatinine) before starting certain first-line ARVs?

options.A: Drugs like tenofovir can affect renal function and require safe dosing
options.B: It proves whether the patient has active tuberculosis infection
options.C: Good kidney function guarantees the patient will never miss a dose
options.D: Kidney tests tell the nurse how many CD4 cells the patient has left

explanation: You're right! Some drugs like Tenofovir can put stress on the kidneys, so checking baseline labs ensures the medication is completely safe for that patient's body. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h5)

question: A newly diagnosed patient wants to start ARVs right away, but tests show they have active meningitis. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Switch the patient to herbal remedies instead of modern drugs
options.B: Refuse to give any counseling because the patient is too sick
options.C: Start the medication immediately without waiting for any other tests
options.D: Support delaying ART briefly while the acute meningitis is treated

explanation: Correct! For serious infections like meningitis, doctors treat the acute infection first before starting ART to prevent dangerous inflammation reactions in the immune system. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h5)

question: What is the main lab test used to check if an ART medication is working successfully?
explanation: Spot on! The viral load test directly counts how much HIV is floating in the blood, giving us the clearest picture of how well the drugs are doing their job. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following is part of routine safety monitoring for someone on long-term ARVs?

options.A: Performing a daily chest X-ray to look for bone fractures
options.B: Repeating HIV testing every single week to see if the virus is gone
options.C: Checking kidney and liver function tests regularly alongside clinical screenings
options.D: Checking the patient's blood pressure only when they report chest pain

explanation: Well done! Since ARVs are processed by the body over years, we run periodic liver and kidney lab tests to catch any organ strain early. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h6)

question: Which side effect do many patients report during the first few weeks of taking an Efavirenz-based regimen?
explanation: Correct! Efavirenz can temporarily cause quirky side effects like vivid dreams or feeling dizzy, but these usually fade away after the first few weeks. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h7)

question: Why is it so important for nurses to check for drug interactions between ART and other medications?

options.A: Other medications will instantly turn HIV into a completely different virus
options.B: Patients are forbidden from taking pain relief while on ARVs
options.C: Liver enzyme interactions can dangerously lower or raise drug levels in the blood
options.D: Taking two pills at once causes them to physically dissolve in the throat

explanation: Spot on! ARVs interact with liver enzymes. If we aren't careful, another drug can accidentally wash the ARVs out too fast or build them up to toxic levels. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h7)

question: What minimum level of medication adherence is needed to keep HIV fully suppressed over the long term?
explanation: You got it! HIV treatment requires consistency. Taking at least 95% of doses on schedule keeps the virus cornered and unable to fight back. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h8)

question: A stable patient complains that monthly clinic visits for pill refills make them miss work and spend too much on transport. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Require the patient to come to the clinic twice a week instead
options.B: Scold the patient for not prioritizing clinic visits over their job
options.C: Enroll the patient in a multi-month dispensing program if they are stable
options.D: Tell the patient they can stop taking their medication entirely

explanation: Brilliant! Multi-month dispensing gives stable patients several months of drugs at once, saving them transport money and protecting their daily work life. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h8)
